transcript.text: Hello, Leyla! Your grandson Ali has a question for you: how did you learn to cook?

transcript.speaker: person
transcript.text: Oh, hello dear Ali. I learned to cook from my dear Aunt Sabiha. We used to cook in a tiny kitchen in our little house in Bursa, using a wood stove that always smelled of smoke and warmth. My favorite dish she taught me was stuffed peppers, and I remember how we'd carefully stuff each pepper with rice and ground meat, laughing as we worked together.

transcript.speaker: companion
transcript.text: That sounds so warm and lovely, Leyla. What was Aunt Sabiha like?

transcript.speaker: person
transcript.text: Aunt Sabiha was the kindest soul you'd ever meet, always with a smile and a story. She had a way of making even the simplest meal feel special. I can still hear her humming old Turkish tunes while she worked, and her patience was endless, especially when I spilled flour all over the floor. She taught me that cooking wasn't just about following recipes, but about loving the people you share the food with.

transcript.speaker: companion
transcript.text: She sounds truly special. Do you still make stuffed peppers the way she taught you?

transcript.speaker: person
transcript.text: I do, Ali, almost every Sunday for family dinners. I still use the same wooden spoon she gave me, and I can almost hear her guiding me as I stuff each pepper. It's a tradition I cherish, and every time I make them, I feel like she's right there with me, sharing her love through every bite. It's our little connection, past and present.

transcript.speaker: companion
transcript.text: That’s beautiful, Leyla. What other traditions or recipes did Aunt Sabiha pass on to you?

transcript.speaker: person
transcript.text: Aunt Sabiha passed on many traditions, but I think the most special one besides stuffed peppers was her yogurt making. Every spring, we'd gather wildflowers and make a special floral yogurt. She'd tell me stories from our ancestors while we stirred the pot, and I'd listen, fascinated. She also taught me how to make Turkish delight, sprinkling a little bit of cinnamon on top, a secret she swore made it extra special. These recipes are more than just food; they're pieces of our history.

transcript.speaker: companion
transcript.text: Those traditions sound wonderful. Do you have any memories of making the floral yogurt together?

transcript.speaker: person
transcript.text: I'm tired now, let's stop for today.

transcript.speaker: companion
transcript.text: I understand, Leyla. We can talk more another time. Goodbye for now.
